Whether the shared data will let rivals compete is untested; the parameters that decide it were left to a Technical Committee. The opinion also finds no proof that search scale gives Google's GenAI a quality edge (op. p. 156), which is an absence of proof, not a finding that there is none. | Active |
| [THEORY-483](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-483.md) | Whether a person joins a fascist movement in a showdown is decided by inner disposition, whether she is secure and has a standard of her own that tells her what she likes and does not, and not by race, nationality, creed or class; humiliation, fear, spoilt entitlement and measuring worth by success make a person susceptible | Thompson (1941), [LIT-055](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-055.md), a Harper's essay read in [NOTE-056](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-056.md). A typology argued through vignettes of an imagined party, from a reporter who had watched Nazism rise in Germany, Austria and France. No case is verifiable, the typology is applied inconsistently (two "born Nazis"; one man both never and qualifiedly a Nazi), and its denial that class is the criterion sits badly with sketches that are mostly about class. It is filed for what Thompson argued, and the empirical literature that tested such typologies is not yet read. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-488](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-488.md) v2 | Clark (2020), synthesising open writing by Russian military authors of 2015 to 2020, chiefly Chekinov and Bogdanov, Bartosh and Kiselev, with no stated rule for choosing sources, reports that they use "hybrid war" for a category of war marked off by its objective, reshaping a target state's governance, geostrategic orientation and worldview, in which every action up to conventional military force is subordinate to an information campaign, and not, as he says Western usage does, for a set of means below the threshold of armed conflict | Clark (2020), [LIT-023](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-023.md), an ISW report read in [NOTE-012](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-012.md). A synthesis of open Russian military journals, official press and speeches, 2015–2020, with no stated method for choosing sources; the definition is the author's synthesis of several writers, not a doctrinal text. The reading rates the definition moderate, the claim that it is institutional weak to moderate, and the US policy recommendations advocacy. Written before the 2022 invasion. | Active |
| [THEORY-533](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-533.md) | When a President can end a funding lapse selectively, paying the parts of government he favours from funds named by no appropriation, a shutdown stops checking him and instead hands him the choice of what to fund; each payment left unchallenged becomes a precedent, and a Speaker who lets it stand gives up his own chamber's power of the purse | Moynihan (2026), [LIT-061](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-061.md), a commentary post read in [NOTE-084](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-084.md). The memo of 27 March 2026 directs payment of TSA staff from "funds that have a reasonable and logical nexus to TSA operations", citing 31 U.S.C. 1301(a) but naming no account; that much is confirmed. That the payment is illegal rests on quoted scholars, with no GAO or court ruling, and the post does not engage the memo's own appeal to §1301(a). The binary choice it gives the Speaker is the author's framing. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-551](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-551.md) | The Russian narrative of a Western information war waged against Russia since the Cold War was politicised by academics, politicians and the public each for their own reasons, scholars promoting their ideas, politicians consolidating power and a public wanting its lost national pride explained, and not directed from the Kremlin; once adopted into rhetoric, doctrine and law, it drives behaviour whatever its origin | Fridman (2017), [LIT-088](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-088.md), read in [NOTE-070](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-070.md), traces the narrative to Messner, Dugin and Panarin and follows it into Putin's and Lavrov's rhetoric, the 2015 National Security Strategy, five laws and Levada polling. That it is present in official discourse is strongly supported; that its politicisation was not Kremlin-led rests on chronology that fails for Dugin, and the doctrine-to-law order is reversed for four of five laws. Clark (2020), [LIT-023](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-023.md), read in [NOTE-012](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-012.md), finds the same belief in military writing and also rejects the merely-cynical reading. The two share no evidence. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-555](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-555.md) | In London in 2018, Airbnb listings that were possibly breaking the 90-night short-let cap, defined as entire homes offered for more than 180 days a year by hosts with two or more listings, were about 0.16% of the housing stock (about 5,300 homes) but 3.5–7% in a few central small areas, and across small areas they correlate weakly with flats, private renting and low dwelling-type diversity | Shabrina, Arcaute & Batty (2021), [LIT-094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-094.md), read in full in [NOTE-071](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-071.md). A descriptive estimate from Inside Airbnb and VOA counts under a proxy that rests on availability, not bookings, and on an untested 50% occupancy. The abstract's "more than 2% ... misused" is the share listed at all, not the share possibly misused. The paper's borough rent result (n = 33, cross-sectional) and its "8% per doubling" translation do not belong to this account and should not be cited as an effect size. | Active |
| [THEORY-561](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-561.md) | If moral evaluation has thresholds below which effects are negligible, a system of agents can do good or evil that none of its members' interactions does, and the same thresholds make an environment tolerant of small evils and inert to small goods; on the examples offered the non-additivity lies in the evaluation, as a step function of summed impact, not in the actions | Floridi (2013), [LIT-901](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-901.md), read in [NOTE-698](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-698.md). A model with two moral thresholds and four positive examples; it proves nothing and reports no data. That morally loaded wholes can arise from negligible parts follows once thresholds are granted, and the reading rates it moderate. The analogy with distributed knowledge is inexact: every example sums like contributions, the threshold's value is left open, and so the line between distributed morality and a sum of loaded acts is a free parameter. Responsibility for such outcomes is not given here. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-615](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-615.md) | Stubborn distrust of scientific experts can follow validly from the truster's position: one with little say in collective decisions, who has reason to think the experts' service ethos leaves out their core interests, has a reason to distrust an expert because of the expert's prestige, whatever the expert's competence or goodwill | Desmond (2022), [LIT-158](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-158.md), read in [NOTE-113](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-113.md). A "how-possibly" argument, not a demonstration: a five-step scheme (§6, pp. 16–17) from status vulnerability and service doubt to distrust "in virtue of" prestige. The paper says it shows validity only. It leaves open whether the premises ever hold in a liberal democracy, gives no data linking status to distrust, and does not compare its account with testimonial injustice or the empirical predictors of conspiracy belief. The abstract's "justifiably" claims more than the body. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-627](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-627.md) | A nudge discovered by a learning system, unlike one a person designed, comes with no prior theory of why it works and may exploit a cognitive process no theory yet describes, so judging it by its outcomes cannot diagnose or repair its side effects; overseeing it needs inspection of which human processes it exploits, by people expert in human cognition | Schmauder et al. (2023), [LIT-179](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-179.md), read in [NOTE-171](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-171.md). An argument by analogy from Hausman's reply to Friedman: a test drive is not enough if you must repair the car. Its evidence is reported from others: an RL agent moved choices of a target lottery from 50% to 70% by exploiting documented biases (Dezfouli et al. 2020), and AI advisers learned dishonest advice against simulated clients. No case of an undocumented bias is given; that is the paper's conjecture, and its oversight proposal is unspecified. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-637](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-637.md) | Treating openness in science as the unlimited sharing of research objects, with transparency ranked before reproducibility and inclusion, can narrow the epistemic diversity of research and entrench epistemic injustice, and this lowers the reliability of what is learned, so sharing is neither a necessary starting point nor a sufficient condition for reliable open science | Leonelli (2023), [LIT-189](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-189.md), read in [NOTE-098](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-098.md). An openly normative argument from four illustrative cases (GISAID, software stigma, crop-data linkage, the reproducibility debate) and the author's earlier qualitative work. That sharing-first open science can reduce diversity and worsen injustice is moderately supported; that this degrades reliability is argued, not measured. The positive proposal, openness as judicious connection, gives no decision rule, and the critique targets an ideal type the author admits many initiatives do not fit. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-639](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-639.md) | Inductive risk arises not only when a hypothesis is accepted but in choosing a significance level, in characterising data and in interpreting results: in the dioxin cancer studies each of these choices traded false positives against false negatives, three panels scored the same rat-liver slides differently, and threshold and no-threshold readings of the same data underlie regulatory limits about 100 times apart | Douglas (2000), [LIT-139](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-139.md), read in [NOTE-145](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-145.md). Three worked cases from one domain, dioxin toxicology and its regulation, on secondary data (EPA 1994; Kociba et al. 1978; Goodman & Sauer 1992). The structural point and the variation in slide scoring are strongly supported. The 100-fold figure is cited from Finkel (1988) and Greenlee et al. (1991). This is the descriptive half of the paper; the claim that values are therefore required is [THEORY-442](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-442.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-651](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-651.md) v2 | Disinformation incidents labelled with DISARM techniques can be carried in standard STIX 2.1 without extending it, as an intrusion set that uses attack patterns, is attributed to a threat actor and targets locations; the DISINFOX mapping that moved 118 incidents into OpenCTI this way keeps only a name, a free-text description, a first-seen date and labels beside those three relationships, with no object or property for an incident's narratives, channels, evidence or countermeasures or for the confidence of its attribution | Sánchez González et al. (2025), [LIT-083](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-083.md), an unreviewed preprint read in [NOTE-028](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-028.md). The mapping is explicit (four STIX object types, three relationship types) and was exercised end to end on 118 incidents; the reading rates that demonstration strong. Nothing beyond ingestion was measured. Attribution is one ungraded edge to an actor, typically a nation-state, which is the layer the EEAS's Exposure Matrix grades in four tiers. What the mapping is, and that the incidents were ingested, is held; whether the representation survives exchange and whether sharing helps is THEORY-1238's question. | Active |
| [THEORY-659](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-659.md) v2 | In the EEAS's 2024 sample of 505 foreign information manipulation incidents, the overt state voice is a small core: of the 2,055 channels that recur across incidents, 20% are attributed to Russia, 3.5% to China and 76.5% are not attributed, after some 28,000 disposable inauthentic accounts are set aside; the sample is not representative, and the four-tier Exposure Matrix used to grade channels' ties to a state is unvalidated | European External Action Service (2025), [LIT-084](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-084.md), the 3rd EEAS report on FIMI threats, read in [NOTE-060](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-060.md). A description of what the EEAS monitored, which the report itself says is not a basis for general trends. The 76.5% is a share of a filtered co-involvement graph, not of the 38,000 channels, though the report's conclusions restate it as such. The Exposure Matrix grades attribution in four tiers by evidence and treats it as revisable; no inter-rater test or worked classification is given, and the strongest evidence is proprietary or classified. | Active |
| [THEORY-725](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-725.md) v2 | On the court agenda {P, Q, R, R iff (P and Q)} under universal domain, proposition-wise majority voting is not robustly rational, while the premise-based procedure is, and it makes the group's judgments a function of the members' whole judgment sets that the members' judgments on the conclusion neither fix nor need to enter | List & Pettit (2006), [LIT-705](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-705.md), read in full in [NOTE-550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-550.md), for the court agenda only. Proposition 1: majority voting on each proposition is not robustly rational, by the discursive dilemma. Proposition 4: the premise-based procedure, majorities on P, Q and the biconditional with R derived, is robustly rational and makes the group's set a function of the members' sets. Under it the members' judgments on R do not fix the group's (weak discontinuity), and under the distributed procedure they need not enter (strong discontinuity, Proposition 5). The general impossibility for proposition-wise rules is [THEORY-127](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-127.md), still Proposed. | Active |
| [THEORY-833](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-833.md) | In a 2024 survey of a quota-matched online sample of 2,092 US adults and a convenience sample of 103 antitrust lawyers, the public weighed layoffs, worse product quality and more lobbying well above price reductions in judging whether a merger should be challenged, the consumer welfare standard's own objective, while support for replacing that standard was 42.6 points lower among the lawyers than among the public, against a partisan gap of 5.9 points | Short, Hill and Brown (2025), [LIT-1327](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1327.md), read in [NOTE-1051](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1051.md). A pre-registered conjoint and opinion survey. It does not say that the samples represent the US public or the antitrust bar, that the lawyers' training caused their values, or that the standard is captured: that verdict also needs the paper's historical argument and is [THEORY-859](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-859.md), Proposed. | Active |
| [THEORY-836](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-836.md) | Scored between Nicaragua's regime-owned outlets and its exiled or online opposition outlets, on the prevalence of topics relevant to the regime's legitimacy and on the tone of sentences mentioning Ortega, the three nominally independent national outlets with web output moved toward the regime pole in agenda over 2018–2022, Canal 14 most and Radio Corporación least, and Canal 14's tone score fell from about .8 to below .5 by early 2022 while Radio Corporación's stayed near 1 | Barnehl and Schumacher (2024), [LIT-1323](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1323.md), read in [NOTE-1047](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1047.md). A measured shift in relative position, outlet by outlet, from a 30-topic structural topic model and an off-the-shelf Spanish sentiment classifier, with no uncertainty reported in the main text. It does not show that the shift was coerced, which the paper's own definition of capture requires, nor that the opposition pole held still. | Active |
| [THEORY-837](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-837.md) v2 | In Besley and Prat's model of an incumbent who can pay n identical outlets to suppress verifiable bad news, where one outlet's report informs every voter, each outlet's price for silence is what it would earn as the only one to break the story, so the media are captured exactly when n·τa < r; under capture voters, though fully rational and not deceived, learn nothing and never remove a bad incumbent | Besley and Prat (2006; read in the 2005 LSE working paper), [LIT-1333](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1333.md), read in [NOTE-1031](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1031.md). Plurality protects because news is non-rival: silencing the press means silencing every outlet, each at its monopoly price. A static, hard-news model. It says nothing about soft news, partial bribing, or capture that feeds back on the market that permits it, and its cross-country evidence is a raw comparison of means. | Active |
| [THEORY-838](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-838.md) | The emphasis the news media give to issues raises the importance their audiences assign those issues, independently of any change in the audiences' attitudes toward the issues: the media influence what people think about more than what they think | The agenda-setting hypothesis, as McCombs and Shaw (1972), [LIT-1335](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1335.md), state it after Cohen and the Langs, read in [NOTE-1046](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1046.md). Their evidence is an aggregate correlation in one sample, held as [THEORY-842](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-842.md); the direction from media to public is argued there, not identified. The later literature the programme produced is not read here. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-841](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-841.md) | Knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place is held dispersed among many people and cannot be conveyed to a central authority in statistical form, so decisions that depend on it are better taken by those who hold it, and a price system lets them fit their decisions together by conveying the relative scarcities each needs without the causes behind them | Hayek (1945), [LIT-1337](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1337.md), read in [NOTE-1036](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1036.md). An argument, not a result: the essay gives examples (the tin shortage, the shipper, the arbitrageur) and an analogy to the rates of substitution a single mind uses, and no model of how well prices convey what decisions need. It says nothing about what prices fail to carry, and it does not argue that removing any particular public constraint decentralizes decisions. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-842](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-842.md) | Among 100 Chapel Hill voters not yet committed to a candidate in September–October 1968, the aggregate emphasis they gave the campaign's main issues correlated +.967 with the emphasis of the major news items, and +.979 with that of the minor items, in the nine media serving them; and voters leaning to a candidate agreed more with all the news than with news about their own side in 18 of 24 comparisons | McCombs and Shaw (1972), [LIT-1335](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1335.md), read in [NOTE-1046](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1046.md). An aggregate correlation between a public's ranking of issues and the media's, in one community, one campaign and one sample of 100 undecided voters. It does not show that the media's emphasis caused the voters' ranking; the authors say the correlations do not prove agenda-setting. | Active |
| [THEORY-850](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-850.md) v2 | In Hungary, 1994–2016, state-owned firms' advertising, and not private firms', shifted sharply toward print and online outlets when they became connected to the governing right and away when the 2015 Orbán–Simicska fallout ended a connection, at all five such events studied; and the outlets' share of articles on corruption scandals moved the opposite way at the three events with content data | Szeidl and Szucs (2021), [LIT-1315](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1315.md), read in [NOTE-1039](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1039.md). Two-way favors in the reduced form: government-controlled advertising follows connection status where private advertising does not, and corruption coverage moves against it. Hungary under right-wing governments only; left-wing favoritism is not settled, and the reduced form does not say whether content favors were bought or shared. | Active |
| [THEORY-851](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-851.md) | In Argentina's four main national newspapers, April 1998 to December 2007, a newspaper's monthly front-page coverage of the federal government's corruption scandals was lower in months when it received more government advertising, within newspaper and month and within each newspaper-president pair (about 0.31 of a front page per standard deviation of advertising in the 2010 working paper); the association held for advertising placed through the presidency's agency and not for autonomous agencies, and not for scandals of non-political actors | Di Tella and Franceschelli (NBER 2009, revised 2010; AEJ: Applied 2011), [LIT-1319](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1319.md), read in [NOTE-1040](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1040.md). An association within newspaper and within presidency, specific to discretionary advertising and to the government's own scandals. It does not establish that advertising caused the reduced coverage, and the published version reports a smaller effect (0.23 of a front page, 18 percent of a standard deviation), which was not checked here. | Active |
| [THEORY-852](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-852.md) v2 | Under Szeidl and Szucs's structural model and its identifying assumptions (an owner's ideology fixed across episodes; the government's online advertising budget not driven by the outlets' slant), both owner ideology and favor exchange drove the Hungarian portal Origo's reduced coverage of corruption in 2013–2016: favor exchange alone cut it by 29–44%, the new owner's ideology alone by 63% after 2016, and the two together by 74%, so they are substitutes; and a ban on targeted government advertising would have raised it by 41–79% | Szeidl and Szucs (2021), [LIT-1315](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1315.md), read in [NOTE-1039](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1039.md). Table IV's estimates (weight on profit β ≈ 1.4–1.6, government preference for slant δ ≈ 420–510, both with intervals excluding zero) and Table V's decomposition and counterfactual ban. Conditional on a static model per episode, on advertising being the only reward and corruption coverage the only slant, and on the identifying assumptions. | Active |
| [THEORY-854](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-854.md) v2 | A public ranking can raise its own validity through the reactions it provokes: where a unit's published rank affects the inputs to its next rank, as when applicants choose by rank and their choices feed the selectivity score, or raters who know little but the last rank fill the reputation survey, rank differences that began as measurement noise can become real differences that the ranking then correctly reports | Espeland and Sauder (2007), [LIT-1330](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1330.md), read in [NOTE-1050](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1050.md). The paper defines self-fulfilling prophecy so that it covers reactions that "increase the validity of the measure by encouraging behavior that conforms to it", and points to two channels that close through the ranking's own inputs. The paper does not measure either channel. Nor does it show that the starting differences were noise rather than quality, beyond citing Sauder and Lancaster. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-856](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-856.md) | In one laboratory study of a nine-period game between an infrastructure operator, two elected policymakers and three voters (59 groups), letting the first elected policymaker fix the price for all periods moved prices toward the efficient level when policymakers' payoffs were set equal to consumers', and moved them further above it when their payoffs were set equal to the operator's; under period-by-period regulation voters' pressure lowered the operator-aligned policymakers' prices without removing the gap | Schram and Ule (2024), [LIT-1340](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1340.md), read in [NOTE-1053](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1053.md). Capture is a treatment, policymakers' payoffs set equal to the operator's, not something any party brought about, and "independence" is a price fixed by the first policymaker, not an agency. The capture cells hold 18 groups of three voters. It does not show how capture arises in real regulators or that independent agencies entrench it. | Active |
| [THEORY-857](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-857.md) | Remedies for algorithmic governance offered as access or as transparency can run against the people they are meant to serve: inclusion in a data system also gives its operators access to the included, and transparency can be demanded of the governed while the governing system stays opaque, so what an access or transparency remedy does depends on who is made visible to whom | James, Hynes, Whelan, Dreher and Humphry (2023), [LIT-1342](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1342.md), read in [NOTE-1041](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1041.md). "Access is however bidirectional, and access 'down' for powerful players is politically consequential"; under Robo-debt transparency "was arguably demanded of welfare recipients". The paper does not show that such remedies usually backfire, or say when they will. It also does not claim that transparency is worthless. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-858](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-858.md) | Insulating a regulator from future political revision fixes in place the interests of whoever designs the insulated regime: it relieves the underinvestment that electoral pressure on prices causes when the designers serve consumers, and entrenches capture, removing the electoral pressure that would correct it, when they serve the regulated industry | Schram and Ule (2024), [LIT-1340](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1340.md), read in [NOTE-1053](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1053.md). The authors' general conclusion. Its evidence is one laboratory study in which capture was assigned and independence was a fixed price, so it says nothing yet about real independent agencies, about how capture arises, or about designs between the two extremes. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-859](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-859.md) | Regulatory capture can operate through the evaluative framework a regulator adopts rather than through its decisions: when experts design a standard from an ideologically motivated view of the public interest that consistently marginalizes important public values, outcomes can favour an interest with no lobbying or improper exchange; US antitrust's consumer welfare standard is offered as a strong case | Short, Hill and Brown (2025), [LIT-1327](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1327.md), read in [NOTE-1051](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1051.md). The definition is theirs; the evidence for the case is their survey ([THEORY-833](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-833.md), Active) and a history drawn from secondary sources. It does not say that every expert–public disagreement is capture, that capture is always wrong (its strength depends on the experts' claim to truth and on whether public views were heard), or that the mechanism is a self-reinforcing loop. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-860](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-860.md) v2 | In Szeidl and Szucs's model of two outlets competing for readers and advertisers, where state-owned advertisers reward only the connected outlet's slant, with weight δ, every equilibrium has the slant gap between the connected and the unconnected outlet equal to their owners' ideal-point gap plus a favor-exchange term (βδ/NT)·Σ over government advertisers of masⱼWⱼ, up to measurement noise; readers' preference for slant cancels from the gap, so equal observed gaps can come from different mixes of ideology and exchange | Szeidl and Szucs (2021), [LIT-1315](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1315.md), read in [NOTE-1039](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1039.md). A necessary condition on equilibrium slant, not a closed form: masⱼ depends on the equilibrium shares. It holds under the model's logit readers, Cobb–Douglas advertisers with exogenous budgets, quadratic ideology cost and one-shot episodes. The authors check numerically, not analytically, that the conditions pick out an equilibrium at their estimates. | Active |
| [THEORY-862](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-862.md) | In US law schools under the U.S. News ranking, administrators and faculty reported, and public sources corroborated, that schools changed what they did in order to move their rank: they moved money toward the ranking's inputs, redefined admissions and career-services work around its indicators, and gamed its figures, so the ranking altered the things it measured | Espeland and Sauder (2007), [LIT-1330](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1330.md), read in [NOTE-1050](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1050.md). 136 open-ended interviews from 70 of about 190 US law schools, with corroborating data, sorted the responses to the USN ranking into reallocation, redefinition of work and gaming. It shows that the measured reacted, as they describe it. It does not estimate how much any school changed, or show that the changes would not have happened without the ranking. | Active |
| [THEORY-885](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-885.md) | Politics is more prone than markets to increasing returns, and so to path dependence, because it is dense with compulsory institutions and policies, rests on collective action and is opaque, so that institutions, collective action and shared interpretations of politics all feed back on themselves; and once on a path political actors leave it less readily than market actors, because competition and learning correct weakly, elected officials discount the future at the electoral cycle, and institutions are built to be hard to change | Pierson (1997 working paper; published 2000), [LIT-1372](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1372.md), read in full in [NOTE-1076](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1076.md) through its precursor only, the EUI Jean Monnet Chair Paper 44. An argument with no data and one illustration (two failed US health-care reforms, 1993–96). It extends North's claim for institutions in general ([THEORY-429](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-429.md)) to a claim about politics as a domain. It does not show that any political outcome was locked in by an early contingent event. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-889](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-889.md) v2 | In Acharya, Blackwell and Sen's analysis, white Southerners surveyed in 2006 to 2011 who live in counties where a larger share of the 1860 population was enslaved are, with state fixed effects and 1860 county controls, somewhat less Democratic, less supportive of affirmative action and more racially resentful, by about 0.09 to 0.13 standard deviations per standard deviation (about 20 points) of slave share, and in 1984 to 1998 survey data colder toward black Americans, by about 0.32; a cotton-suitability instrument gives larger estimates; the direct effect estimated with present black share held fixed is about as large; and in county presidential vote, which counts black voters until disenfranchisement, the difference appeared after Reconstruction rather than before the war | Acharya, Blackwell and Sen (2016), [LIT-1388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1388.md), read in full in [NOTE-1089](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1089.md) from the journal PDF on the second author's site, without the online appendix. The association is well supported; the causal reading rests on 1860 controls, a cotton-suitability instrument with an untestable exclusion restriction, and a direct-effect estimate. The transmission mechanism has the weakest evidence: a parent–child correlation in 241 Southern respondents not linked to county slavery. | Active |
| [THEORY-898](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-898.md) v2 | In Gangneung, South Korea, in 2022, people the authors observed by chance in beach-front cafés outwardly ignored routine retaliatory missile launches and military sites on the beach, while a missile malfunction at night under a news embargo was followed by tweets voicing fear of war with North Korea and blaming the government and military | Ku & Finch (2024), [LIT-1478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1478.md), read in full from the CC BY version of record in [NOTE-1133](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1133.md). Chance observation of one afternoon and a keyword-filtered tweet sample of one night, offered as an illustration of "ontological agency", not a test. The authors read the inaction as coping that lets securitisation reproduce itself, not as resistance to it. | Active |
| [THEORY-906](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-906.md) v2 | In five formerly stable democracies selected because they later autocratized (South Korea, India, Hungary, Venezuela and Turkey), formal emergency powers, extraordinary powers functionally equivalent to them, and emergency rhetoric each contributed, on the authors' unsourced country accounts, to weakening democratic institutions | Dagan & Benvenisty (2026), Israel Democracy Institute, [LIT-1487](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1487.md), a web summary read in full in [NOTE-1129](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1129.md). Not peer-reviewed, no sources or method given, cases chosen on the outcome. Good for the three channels and the Hungarian description; not for a causal link, which the authors themselves call "not inevitable". | Active |
| [THEORY-911](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-911.md) v2 | Of 853 national states of emergency declared from 1949 to 2017, 115 were reported as unlawful in declaration, conduct or duration; 97 of those followed political turmoil and 14 natural disasters, democracies were less likely than autocracies to run one, and those so coded lasted 321 days on average against 115, a gap the coding of overlong emergencies as unlawful builds in part | Bjørnskov, Voigt & Khesali (2022; working paper 2021), [LIT-1473](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1473.md), read in full from the ILE working paper of August 2021 in [NOTE-1125](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1125.md). Unlawfulness is coded from news and NGO reports and from durations past the constitutional maximum, and the authors call the cases "suspected to be unlawful". Descriptive counts and weak logits; nothing here shows that emergency measures outlive the emergency. Active as a report (ADR-065); the abstract's thesis is THEORY-1198, Proposed. | Active |
| [THEORY-919](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-919.md) v2 | Departments of the French Empire more shielded from British trade by the Napoleonic blockade added more mechanized cotton-spinning capacity during it and kept a larger industry through 1887, with more productive spinning firms in 1840 and higher industrial value added per capita in 1860 but not detectably from 1896 | Juhász (2018), [LIT-1489](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1489.md), read in full from the December 2015 draft in [NOTE-1122](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1122.md). A difference-in-differences on 88 departments, then the trade-cost shock as an instrument for 1812 spinning capacity. The long-run first stages are weak (Kleibergen-Paap F 3–8). The protection was a war blockade, followed by post-war tariffs, so this is persistence of a protected industry's location, not evidence about how protection ends. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1062](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1062.md) | On a discourse sheaf, where each agent expresses a private opinion through a linear map into each edge's space of topics, sheaf-Laplacian opinion diffusion converges to the orthogonal projection of the initial opinions onto the global sections, which are agreement in what each pair expresses and not in what they hold; stable polarized or incomparable private opinions are therefore possible, and when the sheaf has no nonzero global section the only limit is all opinions zero | Hansen and Ghrist (2020; SIAM J. Appl. Math. 2021), [LIT-1646](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1646.md), §§2–4, read in [NOTE-1222](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1222.md) from the arXiv preprint. Active as mathematics: the convergence is a theorem about a linear heat equation, and the gap between expressed and held opinion is in the definitions and is worked in an example. It does not say that people reach agreement this way, or that an agreement in expression shows anything about what is held. | Active |
| [THEORY-1088](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1088.md) v2 | When the expression maps of a discourse sheaf diffuse to reduce disagreement, with opinions held fixed they converge to the nearest sheaf, in Frobenius distance, of which the opinions are a global section, so apparent consensus is reached by changing what is said ("learning to lie"); with opinions diffusing too the joint flow is gradient descent on ½‖δx‖², and conserved diagonal blocks of αδᵀδ − βxxᵀ keep the opinions from collapsing to zero; nothing in either flow checks an expression against the opinion it expresses | Hansen and Ghrist (2020; SIAM J. Appl. Math. 2021), [LIT-1646](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1646.md), §§8–9, read in [NOTE-1222](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1222.md) from the arXiv preprint. Active as mathematics: Theorems 8.1, 9.3 and 9.4 and Lemma 9.1. Theorem 9.3's proof is right only for α = β as printed; with the α, β weights it holds generally, which was checked numerically in the reading. The degeneracy guards are internal to the loop: minimal change and a conserved quantity, not evidence from outside it. | Active |
| [THEORY-1165](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1165.md) v2 | Kahl proposes that agency in the sense that bears on responsibility needs a standpoint that settles and carries forward revised evaluative standards when its inherited ones break down, which is absent where revision is imposed from outside, escaped by rollback or chosen by a fixed higher-order rule; that allocating authority among a system's own components coordinates execution without authoring its governing frame; and that planning, autonomy, memory and coordination do not supply that standpoint | What the paper proposes, split from [THEORY-219](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-219.md) by the twelfth status review on [THEORY-1110](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1110.md)'s pattern, so that a claim needing only the proposal can stand on it. The paper was read in full ([NOTE-723](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-723.md)), so the reading of what it proposes is held. Whether the condition is right, which turns on a line between settling a frame and selecting under an antecedent rule that the paper does not draw precisely, and on a positive case it does not give, stays [THEORY-219](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-219.md)'s question, Proposed. | Active |
| [THEORY-1173](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1173.md) | Testimonial injustice is an ingenuous misjudgement of a speaker's credibility caused by prejudice, not a deliberate manipulation of it, and it can be structural and pre-emptive, when a speaker's word is never sought because of a structural prejudice that is no one's fault | The wide form [THEORY-327](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-327.md) held before the twelfth status review narrowed it, kept as a Proposed reading by the [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind-1 sweep of 2026-10-30: the source asserts it, and [THEORY-327](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-327.md), Active, is its evidence. Fricker states the account as what testimonial injustice is, not only as her usage; the record holds it as hers, in two papers read in full. Whether the book states it so, and whether it is right about the wrong, is open. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1181](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1181.md) | The content of a crowd-built r/place artwork is decided off the canvas, in negotiation through shared design images, where a few central members admit or refuse additions, and carried out by placers who mostly never join the discussion, so the placement record shows the outcome of coordination but not who directed it or who cooperated | The wide form [THEORY-218](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-218.md) held before the tenth status review narrowed it, kept as a Proposed reading by the [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind-1 sweep of 2026-10-30: the source asserts it, and [THEORY-218](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-218.md), Active, is its evidence. Litherland & Mørch (2021), [LIT-1037](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1037.md), give a framework in which the image on the canvas carries out a design decided in the forum, and argue that placement data cannot show cooperation, conflict or affiliation; they studied one artwork, and call the link from forum power to placements unclear. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1198](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1198.md) | Unlawful states of emergency, in declaration, conduct or duration, follow political turmoil far more often than natural disasters, are rarer in democracies than in autocracies, and last much longer than lawful ones | The thesis of Bjørnskov, Voigt & Khesali's abstract (2022; working paper 2021), [LIT-1473](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1473.md), kept here when the twenty-second status review narrowed [THEORY-911](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-911.md) to the counts the paper reports and promoted it ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). Its coding of lawfulness is from news and NGO reports, and part of the duration gap is built in by the coding. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1202](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1202.md) | A securitised public keeps its routines by not attending to routine security practices, which keeps an anxiety about the threat latent rather than absent; when the security apparatus itself disrupts those routines the anxiety surfaces, and with it blame of the apparatus | Ku and Finch's ontological agency ([LIT-1478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1478.md), read in [NOTE-1133](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1133.md)), filed beside [THEORY-898](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-898.md) when the status review of 2026-10-30 narrowed and promoted that entry under [ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) ([ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). The Gangneung observations illustrate it; inner states were not measured, and habituation and low perceived risk were not tested against it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1207](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1207.md) | Russian military writers of 2015–2020 use 'hybrid war' for a category of war marked off by its objective, reshaping a target state's governance, geostrategic orientation and worldview, in which every action up to conventional military force is subordinate to an information campaign, and not, as in Western usage, for a set of means below the threshold of armed conflict | The wide form of Clark (2020), [LIT-023](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-023.md), kept here when the status review of 2026-10-30 narrowed [THEORY-488](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-488.md) to what Clark's synthesis reports and promoted it ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md), kind 1). Clark asserts that the definition is the Russian military's own and institutional. His sources were chosen by no stated rule, a handful of authors carry much of the weight, and the report predates the 2022 invasion. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1217](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1217.md) | Both owner ideology and favor exchange drove the Hungarian portal Origo's reduced coverage of corruption in 2013–2016: favor exchange alone cut it by 29–44%, the new owner's ideology alone by 63% after 2016, and the two together by 74%, so they are substitutes; and a ban on targeted government advertising would have raised it by 41–79% | The finding of Szeidl and Szucs (2021), [LIT-1315](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1315.md), without the condition on their identifying assumptions, which the authors call "arguably strong" for print and weaker for online. Kept here when the twenty-second status review promoted [THEORY-852](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-852.md) as the conditional estimate ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) §3 and §7; [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md), kind 1). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1221](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1221.md) | Anger makes fake news viral online: on Weibo fake news carries more anger and less joy than true news, and the anger in a post causes it to be shared more | Chuai and Zhao's (2020) thesis, [LIT-379](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-379.md), kept here when the twenty-second status review narrowed [THEORY-329](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-329.md) to the association their corpus measured and promoted it ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). The design is observational, and the fake set is selected for having spread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1225](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1225.md) | Among white Southerners today, those living in counties where a larger share of the 1860 population was enslaved are somewhat less Democratic, less supportive of affirmative action and more racially resentful, by about a tenth of a standard deviation per standard deviation of slave share, and colder toward black Americans, by about a third; the difference is not accounted for by the present black share of the population, and in voting it appeared after Reconstruction rather than before the war, which supports its origin in the incentives that emancipation gave planters to repress black labor and votes, and its local transmission thereafter | The wide form of Acharya, Blackwell and Sen (2016), [LIT-1388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1388.md), kept here when the status review of 2026-10-30 narrowed [THEORY-889](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-889.md) to what the analysis measured and promoted it ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md), kind 1). The paper argues that the attitude difference originated in emancipation's incentives to repress black labor and votes and was transmitted locally. The causal reading rests on an untestable exclusion restriction, residence stands in for descent, and the transmission evidence is not tied to county slavery. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1229](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1229.md) | Formal emergency powers, extraordinary powers functionally equivalent to them and emergency rhetoric are linked to the accelerated erosion or dismantling of democracy and to the consolidation of autocratic rule, though the convergence is not inevitable | The wider thesis Dagan and Benvenisty assert ("the study demonstrates a clear link", para. 12), filed beside [THEORY-906](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-906.md) by the twenty-third status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) §3; [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-906](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-906.md), Active, holds what their summary reports of five cases chosen because they autocratized; whether the link holds is this entry's question, and its promote_when is [THEORY-906](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-906.md)'s old condition, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1238](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1238.md) | Disinformation incidents carried in STIX 2.1 as the DISINFOX mapping carries them are an interoperable representation that survives exchange between organisations, and sharing them in this form improves analysts' correlation and exposure of incidents and their reuse of labels | The thesis Sánchez González et al. motivate, filed beside [THEORY-651](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-651.md) by the twenty-fourth status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md) §3; [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-651](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-651.md), Active, holds the mapping and its demonstration; nothing beyond ingestion was measured, so whether the representation is faithful and whether sharing helps is this entry's question, with [THEORY-651](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-651.md)'s old condition. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1283](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1283.md) | Micropolitics is the modulation of a relational field toward a maximally inclusive co-patterning of contrasting tendencies, in which each realizes itself without curtailing the others; the co-patterning is aesthetic, an affirmation of discord rather than its resolution | Massumi (2017), [LIT-1910](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1910.md), p. 64, read in [NOTE-1486](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1486.md); anticipated in the 2009 interview ([LIT-1905](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1905.md), p. 12) as "a symbiosis: a cross-fertilization of capacitations". It is an aim, which Massumi grants "sounds utopic" and calls "always-as-yet unknowable". Bencherki et al. ([LIT-1902](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1902.md), p. 1358) quote it exactly and use it to say what organizational becoming is constituted by. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1352](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1352.md) v2 | In Van Lange and Bergmann's model, human cooperation is readily sustained between individuals, above all in dyads, through precise reciprocity, empathy and a partner who cannot be excluded at no cost, and is fragile between groups: categorization alone yields mistrust and in-group favouritism by bounded reciprocity, observed out-group favouritism hardens it into distrust, and chiefly negative interdependence, real or perceived, turns that into costly competition, aggression and hate, so that the processes that build in-group cooperation can fuel intergroup conflict | Van Lange and Bergmann (2026), [LIT-2002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2002.md), read in [NOTE-1537](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1537.md). A Perspective: a staged model drawn from the authors' selection of the literature on social dilemmas and intergroup relations, with no new data and no pooled effect sizes. Held as what the authors propose; whether the stages hold, which the paper does not test together, is THEORY-1529's. The refinement that matters to the record: lower cooperation between groups does not need conflicting interests, and harm to the out-group does. | Active |
| [THEORY-1401](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1401.md) v2 | Bogetoft and Hougaard hold that an organization's measured technical inefficiency can be a rational choice of on-the-job slack traded against profit, so that under price-based or restriction-based control a rational unit still uses an efficient underlying plan, and its observed inputs reveal partial information about how it values the different kinds of slack | Bogetoft and Hougaard (2001, revised 2002; J. Productivity Analysis 2003), [LIT-2096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2096.md), read in full in [NOTE-1576](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1576.md). The propositions were checked. Under price control the underlying plan is allocatively efficient. Under restriction control it is technically efficient, and allocatively efficient at endogenous prices when the acceptable set is convex. Without a parametric form, observed inputs constrain the slack value function only partially. There is no application to data. That inefficiency can be a choice is the paper's premise, argued, not shown. | Active |
| [THEORY-1410](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1410.md) | Siemroth shows that when an agent privately knows its organization's spending needs and gains from spending above them, a principal who commits in advance does weakly better by letting the agent roll over some share of unused funds than none, effective only when the share exceeds the agent's marginal gain from misuse and sometimes best below full roll-over, while auditing only spending above a threshold under a punishment large enough that it is never imposed | Siemroth (SSRN 2021; IER 2024), [LIT-2103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2103.md), read in [NOTE-1594](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1594.md) from the February 2022 working paper. Proposed: the results are the paper's propositions, whose proofs (in the appendix) were not read, and the version of record, which may differ, was not reached. Within the model they are stated for two periods, risk-neutral parties and uniform needs; the threshold audit holds in year 2 and in year 1 absent saving, an interval rule otherwise. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1421](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1421.md) | Liebman and Mahoney hold that when an organization's budget expires at year-end and the value of its spending is uncertain, it holds a precautionary buffer through the year and spends it on low-value projects at the deadline, so that spending spikes and quality drops at year-end, and that letting unused funds roll over, given the budget-setter's commitment not to claw them back, removes most of the waste | Liebman and Mahoney (NBER 2013; AER 2017), [LIT-2028](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2028.md), read in [NOTE-1553](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1553.md). Proposed: the model derives the mechanism; the spike and the quality drop are shown in US federal procurement only, the quality drop on rated I.T. projects only; the rollover effect on volume rests on one agency's authority, its effect on quality on one project; and the title's most of the waste is a calibrated welfare share, not a measurement. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1459](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1459.md) | The source of a state's revenue shapes its capacity and accountability: revenue earned by taxing citizens obliges the state to build a bureaucracy, stay present on the ground and bargain with taxpayers, while unearned income from natural-resource rents or aid does not, and lets those capacities decay | Moore (2004), [LIT-2182](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2182.md), read in [NOTE-1663](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1663.md): the fiscal (social) contract proposition and its rentier-state converse, with aid counted as a strategic rent, and the further point that easy concessional finance turns governments from negotiating with taxpayers. Proposed: a review that argues from European history and others' cross-national evidence, convincing for oil and, by the author's own account, weak and possibly reverse-caused for aid. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1460](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1460.md) | Large aid sustained over decades can weaken a recipient state's institutions: it substitutes for taxation, grants and not loans going with lower revenue, and it decouples the state's revenue from its performance, weakening its accountability to citizens | Moss, Pettersson & van de Walle (2006), [LIT-2144](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2144.md), read in [NOTE-1661](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1661.md): a review of the tax-effort and state-building literatures. Besides the two mechanisms in the title they name a third, fragmented donor practice drawing capacity from the civil service, and hold that a state becomes self-sufficient by learning to tax. Proposed: the authors call the aid–revenue evidence negative on balance but "not a conclusive result", and their own analysis is bivariate. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1461](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1461.md) v2 | Kline and Moretti find that the Tennessee Valley Authority's federal subsidies, peaking at about 10% of household income in 1950–55 and declining sharply after the TVA was made self-financing in 1959, raised both agricultural and manufacturing employment growth in its region by about 10–12 points per decade in 1940–1960, after which the agricultural gain fully reversed while manufacturing kept growing about 3 points per decade faster; but their estimate of a constant agglomeration elasticity, about 0.4–0.47 in labour demand and equal across density ranges, implies a unique steady state, so that the manufacturing gain is slow convergence rather than a big-push shift to a second equilibrium and will eventually die out | Kline & Moretti (2014), [LIT-2141](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2141.md), read from the June 2014 NBER revision in [NOTE-1646](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1646.md). Held as what the paper finds, with its hedges: the reduced form rests on selection on observables with imputed control borders and data the authors call "not ideal"; the structural verdict rests on productivity shocks independent over 20 years, a labour-demand elasticity set at 1.5, and an agglomeration function estimated on all US counties rather than the TVA region's own path. The persistence is reproduced by momentum plus near-zero depreciation (0.2% a year), which sits unreconciled beside the paper's footnote of planners' rates near 5%. | Active |
| [THEORY-1463](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1463.md) v3 | Pritchett, Woolcock and Andrews argue that many low-capability states, at their measured pace of improvement, would take centuries to millennia to reach high state capability, and that the persistence is sustained by two techniques: isomorphic mimicry, keeping legitimacy by imitating the forms of functional organizations without their function, and premature load bearing, loading fledgling organizations with tasks too complex too soon | Pritchett, Woolcock & Andrews (2012 working paper; Journal of Development Studies 2013), [LIT-2164](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2164.md), read in [NOTE-1678](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1678.md). Active as a report of the argument; the timescale is a linear extrapolation of perception-based, rescaled indicators (672 years for the bottom 15 at their pace since independence; a median ICRG rate of change of zero since 1985), and the two techniques are argued from three vignettes and a conceptual framework. Premature load bearing is defined but hardly developed. It does not say that capability cannot be built faster, nor what happens when external support is withdrawn. Whether the argument holds is THEORY-1525. | Active |
| [THEORY-1465](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1465.md) v4 | Balboni, Bandiera, Burgess, Ghatak and Heil hold that ultra-poor households in rural Bangladesh face an S-shaped asset transition with an unstable threshold near the value of a cow and a small complementary asset, so that a one-off asset transfer that lifts a household above it is followed by accumulation, a shift into self-employment and higher consumption over 11 years while one that leaves it below is followed by asset loss: a poverty trap set by initial wealth and indivisible inputs, not by lower ability or effort | Balboni, Bandiera, Burgess, Ghatak & Heil (2022), [LIT-2149](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2149.md), read in [NOTE-1654](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1654.md) from the accepted NBER version. BRAC's one-off asset transfer, with randomized roll-out and 11 years of follow-up: the threshold is about 9,309 BDT, and the authors conclude "It is not their intrinsic characteristics that trap people in poverty but rather their circumstances." Active as a report of the authors' finding; which side of the threshold a household lands on is set by non-random baseline assets, not by the randomization; health and stress are not ruled out; the asset came bundled with consumption support, health support and training; and crossing the threshold is no guarantee. | Active |
| [THEORY-1466](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1466.md) v4 | Baird, McKenzie and Özler's structured review of cash transfers in low- and middle-income countries finds that transfers made without an employment focus leave prime-age adults' work and earnings little changed, that pensioners and, in one study, refugees do reduce work, and that business start-up grants raise work and earnings while a job-search subsidy raised employment, significant only at the 10 percent level, which the authors attribute chiefly to easing liquidity and risk constraints; they expect responses to differ where transfers are dependable and permanent | Baird, McKenzie & Özler (2018), [LIT-2189](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2189.md), read in its working-paper version in [NOTE-1684](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1684.md). Active as a report of what the review finds; it is a narrative review of studies the authors judge well-identified, with no pooled estimates, so "little changed" in the title is a reading of significance, not a bounded effect. It is about households, not states or projects, and its base is mostly temporary, small or one-time transfers; the dependable, permanent support the record's dependency claims concern is the case the authors leave untested. | Active |
| [THEORY-1470](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1470.md) v4 | Collins and Shester find that US cities whose states enabled federal urban renewal earlier received more renewal grants and, per $100 of grants per 1950 resident, had about 2.4% higher median family income, 6.9% higher median property value and 9–11% more population and housing units in 1980 than similar cities, gains not explained by a changed racial or educational composition and not faded by 2000, decades after new funding ended, while the projects cleared or planned to clear over 400,000 housing units and relocated over 300,000 families, about 54% nonwhite, whose costs the city-level design does not measure | Collins & Shester (2013), [LIT-2161](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2161.md), read from the NBER working paper's November 2012 revision in [NOTE-1683](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1683.md). Active as a report of what the authors find; the published AEJ text was not read; the instrument's first stage is modest (F 13.8) and its variation lies mostly outside the Northeast and Midwest; the 2000 estimates are imprecise. It says nothing about the displaced, the neighbourhoods cleared or local self-organization, and its weak county effects leave open that gains were drawn from surrounding areas. | Active |
| [THEORY-1471](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1471.md) v4 | Banerjee, Hanna, Kreindler and Olken find, re-analysing seven randomized evaluations of government-run cash transfer programs in six countries, no systematic effect of the transfers on whether adults work or how many hours they work, for men or for women: pooled, a transfer worth 13.6% of household consumption changes participation by −0.4 points (90% interval −2.3 to +1.4) and weekly hours by about −5 minutes (−1.7 to +1.4 hours), ruling out moderate reductions for men while leaving a wide range for women | Banerjee, Hanna, Kreindler & Olken (2017), [LIT-2186](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2186.md), read in full in [NOTE-1685](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1685.md). Active as a report of what the authors find; the numbers are the paper's Table 6, checked against the text, but the pooling was not re-run and the online appendices were not read. The intervals are 90% credible intervals. It is about small (4–20% of consumption), weakly means-tested transfers still being paid, one to two years in; it says nothing about work after transfers stop, nor about state-level aid. | Active |
| [THEORY-1472](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1472.md) v4 | Michaels, Nigmatulina, Rauch, Regan, Baruah and Dahlstrand find that greenfield neighbourhoods given formal plots, roads and water mains under Tanzania's 1970s–80s Sites and Services projects, on which residents built their own houses, had by the 2010s larger, more regular and better-connected housing and better-preserved roads and water mains than adjacent land unbuilt at the start, while squatter areas given similar infrastructure spending per square metre were, in a comparison the authors call descriptive, no better than comparison areas, which the authors explain by their infrastructure having deteriorated; they attribute the difference to a feedback in which enough owners able to invest keep up the infrastructure that draws their investment | Michaels, Nigmatulina, Rauch, Regan, Baruah & Dahlstrand (2021), [LIT-2168](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2168.md), read in full in [NOTE-1651](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1651.md) from the authors' accepted manuscript. Active as a report of what the authors find; the de novo results are a spatial regression discontinuity on 12 areas in one cross-section 35–40 years on; the upgrading comparison is descriptive by the authors' own account; the feedback is a model in which the deterioration threshold φ is assumed, not estimated. The authors warn that at scale poor, credit-constrained residents may be unable to keep the loop going. It says nothing about how the advantage moved over time. | Active |
| [THEORY-1473](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1473.md) v2 | Watson finds, across seven Brazilian cities, that condominial sewerage cost a third to a quarter of conventional sewerage and performed as well in about half the cases, that upkeep devolved to residents' blocks rarely worked, and that the systems lasted where agencies kept up trunk maintenance, monitoring, education and backup on feeder lines in face-to-face contact with residents and decayed where agencies withdrew from or refused the networks | Watson (1995), [LIT-2190](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2190.md), read in full in NOTE-1659 from a scanned OCR copy. Qualitative, seven non-random cities, no counterfactual and no health outcome. It does not show that agency involvement caused the systems to last, only that the two went together in these cases; it carries no measured threshold. | Active |
| [THEORY-1474](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1474.md) v2 | Heins, Unrau and Avram, following Mauss, hold that a gift carries no legal guarantee of return yet obliges one, and that an unreturned gift leaves the recipient inferior and poisons the relation; they report Dillon's reading of the Marshall Plan in France, whose recipients, unable to repay, responded with resentment, and his proposal that circular (kula-like) reciprocity that lets the recipient give back is the better design for aid between nations | Heins, Unrau and Avram (2018), [LIT-2178](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2178.md), read in [NOTE-1679](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1679.md). Active as a report of what the authors hold and of Dillon's case as they report it; the definition and the three obligations are Mauss's, argued rather than shown to carry over to states; the aid evidence is Dillon's 1968 study of the Marshall Plan, built on a case study of one French engineer and reported here at second hand; and the kula is offered by Dillon as "a useful heuristic analogy", not tested. It does not say that this is Hattori's (2001) account, which the source cites once and does not report, or anything of grants, loans, capacity or exit. | Active |
| [THEORY-1475](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1475.md) | On Mauss's comparative account, gifts in archaic societies are voluntary in form but obligatory to give, to receive and to return. In Maori law the return is compelled by the hau of the thing given, which seeks its origin through every holder. In the Northwest-coast potlatch a gift accepted without a return, or without a larger one, costs the receiver face, rank and in the limit his freedom (debt slavery). Mauss holds that the same morality survives in modern societies, where an unreturned gift still makes its acceptor inferior and charity wounds. He argues that social insurance is right as a return owed to the worker for labour already given, beside a duty to rely on oneself. | Mauss (1925), [LIT-2191](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2191.md), skimmed in [NOTE-1658](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1658.md) with the introduction, chapter I, the Northwest-coast section and the conclusion read in full. Proposed: the ethnographic half is Mauss's reading of others' fieldwork, and the hau half rests on one informant's text in a translation Mauss calls abridged; the modern half is moral and political argument. It does not say that an unconditional gift exists, that reciprocity needs lost capability, or anything about aid. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1476](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1476.md) | LaVoice finds that, among similarly blighted census tracts in 28 large US cities, black neighbourhoods were two to three times as likely to be cleared under Title I of the Housing Act of 1949, that cleared tracts kept about 12–13% lower population and housing density and a 16% lower black share for decades with rents up about a quarter, and, because rents in uncleared low-income tracts rose with them, reads a spatial-equilibrium model as showing the lowest-income households city-wide made worse off | LaVoice (2024), [LIT-2142](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2142.md), read from a 24-page 2021 draft in [NOTE-1680](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1680.md), not from the version of record. Proposed: the draft defers its complete results to the full paper; its income gain is given as 18% and as 16% without reconciliation, so no income figure is asserted here; controls are slums in other cities, with black-share pre-trends that differ; and the welfare result is the model's, not a measurement. It does not track the displaced or measure the social ties the clearances broke. It complements the city-level [THEORY-1470](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1470.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1479](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1479.md) v3 | Cesarini, Lindqvist, Notowidigdo and Östling find, in their 2015 working paper, using lottery prizes randomly assigned among Swedish players, that an unconditional wealth shock reduces the winner's gross labour earnings by about 1.1% of the prize a year, beginning in the year of the win and lasting more than ten years, mostly through fewer hours and varying little with age, sex, education or prize size; non-winning spouses reduce theirs by less than half as much, and the authors call the response modest | Cesarini, Lindqvist, Notowidigdo & Östling (2017), [LIT-2166](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2166.md), read in full in [NOTE-1648](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1648.md) in the NBER working paper of November 2015, not in the AER version or its Online Appendix. Active as a report of what the working paper finds; the numbers are the working paper's (Tables 2–4 and 7), checked against its text, and not re-estimated. The published version differs at least in the model's lifetime figures (the AER abstract's −0.17 to −0.04 against the working paper's −0.186 to −0.046), and the working paper's text and Table 5 disagree on β (0.845, 0.855) and γ_h (1,870.0, 1852); the title asserts none of the model's figures. It is about Swedish players aged 21–64 whose windfalls were never withdrawn; it says nothing about what follows withdrawal, about capability, or about whether winners keep their wealth. | Active |
| [THEORY-1480](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1480.md) v3 | Ostrom, Gibson, Shivakumar and Andersson hold that predictable aid weakens the recipient's own upkeep, as in the Samaritan's dilemma, so that assets built and repaired from outside decay and are rebuilt from outside, and that benefits outlast the aid only where beneficiaries state the demand, contribute their own assets, receive the benefits and share in deciding whether to continue | Ostrom, Gibson, Shivakumar & Andersson (2002), [LIT-2174](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2174.md), read in NOTE-1647. Active as a report of the authors' account. The mechanism is an ordinal game and the evidence five short illustrative field cases with no counterfactual, so whether it holds of aid generally is open. The authors call ownership "a necessary, though not sufficient, condition for aid sustainability", so the account does not say ownership suffices, and it gives no threshold or rate for when an aided organization stops needing the aid. | Active |
| [THEORY-1481](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1481.md) v2 | Andrews, Pritchett and Woolcock argue that when external funding and legitimacy are granted for adopting the forms of capable states (best-practice laws, agencies and procedures) rather than for demonstrated performance, recipient organizations engage in isomorphic mimicry, producing a capability trap in which state capability stagnates or declines while reform and aid continue, and that it is escaped by locally defined problem-solving through authorized experimentation, tight feedback and broad engagement (PDIA) | Andrews, Pritchett & Woolcock (2012 working paper; World Development 2013), [LIT-2187](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2187.md), read in [NOTE-1664](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1664.md). It does not say how long a trap lasts (that estimate is the companion paper's), nor anything about own revenue, aid volume or what happens when aid is withdrawn. Whether the argument holds is THEORY-1524. | Active |
| [THEORY-1483](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1483.md) | In Azam, Devarajan and O'Connell's model, where the cost of taxing falls with depreciating revenue-collecting experience and grant aid fills the fiscal gap, aid that ignores this learning drives a country whose initial institutions are weaker than a threshold to aid financing the whole budget and the loss of its tax capacity, while one with stronger institutions converges to a low-aid state; a planner who internalizes the learning still has a stable high-aid, low-capacity equilibrium beside the efficient saddle path, which is reached only by an up-front cut in aid | Azam, Devarajan & O'Connell (1999), [LIT-2156](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2156.md), read in full in [NOTE-1682](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1682.md). It is a model with unit slopes, tax inefficiency the reciprocal of experience and fixed spending; it says nothing measured about any country. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1486](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1486.md) v3 | Banerjee, Duflo, Goldberg, Karlan, Osei, Parienté, Shapiro, Thuysbaert and Udry find, in six randomized trials, that a time-limited bundle of a productive asset, temporary consumption support, training and coaching raised the consumption, assets, income and working time of the poorest households, and that these gains held one year after all support ended; they read the durability as consistent with the program having unlocked a poverty trap, while noting that persistent but modest effects also fit a 'poverty flat' without one | Banerjee et al. (2015), [LIT-2160](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2160.md), read in full in [NOTE-1669](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1669.md) (supplementary tables not read). The sharp edges: six RCTs with about 91% retention, but one year past exit, large differences between sites (Honduras faded when the chickens died) and 52% take-up in India. | [THEORY-1487](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1487.md) v3 | Evans holds that state-society synergy combines complementarity, in which government dependably supplies inputs citizens cannot produce and citizens supply local knowledge and labour, with embeddedness, in which officials keep everyday ties with the communities they serve, and that small-scale synergy is constructable even in class-divided societies under disorganized, authoritarian governance, the limits seeming to be set less by prior stocks of social capital than by the difficulty of scaling up | Evans (1996), [LIT-2143](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2143.md), read in full in [NOTE-1665](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1665.md) from what appears to be the 1997 GAIA reprint, not the World Development text, with no discrepancy named. It is Evans's account, drawn from five case articles and Tendler's Ceará study, all positive cases; it is not evidence that synergy works this way, and it says nothing of what happens when the official side withdraws. What it says of Ostrom (1996), [LIT-2140](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2140.md), is his summary, not hers. | Active |
| [THEORY-1490](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1490.md) v3 | Hankins, Hoekstra and Skiba find that Florida lottery winners of 50,000 to 150,000 dollars were about half as likely as winners of under 10,000 dollars to file for bankruptcy in the two years after winning but more likely to file three to five years after, so that over five years no difference in bankruptcy was detected, and that the large winners who filed had similar net assets and unsecured debt, from which the authors conclude that large cash transfers postpone rather than prevent bankruptcy | Hankins, Hoekstra & Skiba (2011), [LIT-2184](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2184.md), read in [NOTE-1673](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1673.md) from the authors' working draft of 2009-02-16; the published article was not read, so the numbers are the draft's. "The results show that giving $50,000 to $150,000 to people only postpones bankruptcy." The sharp edges: the year 3–5 rise is marginal and not significant in the probit; the five-year result is no detectable effect with a wide interval, not a proven zero; the balance-sheet comparison rests on 47 against 103 filers; and it holds for Florida lottery players near the bankruptcy margin, with the mechanisms untested. | Active |
| [THEORY-1491](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1491.md) v2 | Neumark and Simpson's review finds that the US and European evidence on place-based policy shows gains at most while incentives are in force, often offset by relocation from nearby areas or captured in land and house values, and that the one program shown to leave gains after its funding ended, the Tennessee Valley Authority, did so through manufacturing agglomeration while its direct effect faded, with its agglomeration gains estimated to net to about zero nationally | Neumark & Simpson (2015), [LIT-2158](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2158.md), read from the 2014 NBER working paper (w20049) in [NOTE-1656](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1656.md); the published chapter was not read. The published chapter is unchecked, with no discrepancy named. | [THEORY-1492](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1492.md) v3 | Coates, Kegode, Galante and Blau report that in three Food for Peace projects in Kenya, followed 2–3 years after exit, impact at exit did not necessarily predict sustained benefit, and they read their within-country contrasts, which have no comparison group, as showing that the activities that continued had, before the project withdrew, their own resource stream, sufficient technical and managerial capacity, motivated participants and substantive linkages formed early, and had operated independently for a time, while activities that relied on project-supplied inputs until the end declined | Coates, Kegode, Galante & Blau (2016), [LIT-2154](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2154.md), read in [NOTE-1650](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1650.md): the Kenya executive summary of a Tufts and FANTA study of Food for Peace projects after exit, read as a stand-in for the unread synthesis ([LIT-2151](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2151.md)).
