| [THEORY-1493](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1493.md) v3 | Banerjee, Duflo and Sharma find, in a randomized trial in West Bengal, that the treatment effects of a one-time Targeting the Ultra Poor package on household consumption, income and health grew for seven years after the asset transfer and persisted to year ten, although the implementer had no contact with households after eighteen months; they attribute the persistence mainly to treated households taking better advantage of wage employment and migration, and hold it consistent with, but not proof of, escape from a poverty trap | Banerjee, Duflo & Sharma (2021), [LIT-2170](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2170.md), read in full in [NOTE-1667](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1667.md) as the NBER working paper (the version of record and the appendix not read). It says nothing about aid to states. | Active |
| [THEORY-1494](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1494.md) v3 | Evans and Popova's count by sign and significance of 44 estimates from 19 studies of conditional and unconditional cash transfers in low- and middle-income countries finds that transfers almost never raise spending on alcohol and tobacco: 82% of the estimates are negative, only two are positive and significant, both non-experimental, none of 17 randomized estimates is positive and significant, and the pattern does not differ between conditional and unconditional programs, across regions or with duration of receipt | Evans & Popova (2017), [LIT-2150](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2150.md), read as the 2014 World Bank working paper in [NOTE-1649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1649.md). | [THEORY-1496](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1496.md) v2 | When two Food for Peace projects in India handed their activities to Government of India programmes, activities continued two years after exit where the receiving programme had dedicated resources, functioning infrastructure and a legal commitment and the project's linkage to it was operating before exit, and stopped where the linkage was begun late; results often varied between states by more than they changed over time | Rogers, Klemeyer, Bondre & Fierstein (2017), [LIT-2148](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2148.md), read in [NOTE-1655](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1655.md): the India executive summary of a Tufts and FANTA study of Food for Peace projects after exit, read as a stand-in for the unread synthesis ([LIT-2151](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2151.md)). The sharp edges: an executive summary with no comparison group and a subset of states, in which the contrast between early and late linkage rests on one late case. | Active |
| [THEORY-1497](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1497.md) v2 | St John holds that Burning Man's gifting carries no obligation on the recipient to reciprocate, yet sustains circulation through gratitude that recipients return to the community in later labour, a generalized rather than bilateral reciprocity, and that perhaps the most pressing threat to it is non-participation, which the organization answered in part by reforming how theme camps are registered and placed | St John (2017), [LIT-2188](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2188.md), read in full in [NOTE-1662](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1662.md). | [THEORY-1499](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1499.md) v3 | Davis and Weinstein find that the Allied bombing of Japanese cities in World War II, which destroyed almost half the structures in the 66 targeted cities, changed relative city size only temporarily: across 303 cities, 1947–60 population growth undid 1940–47 growth instrumented on deaths and buildings destroyed per capita one for one, or by about three-quarters once 1925–40 trend growth is controlled, and wholly by 1965, with Hiroshima and Nagasaki back on their prewar trends; the authors read this as rejecting random growth and as showing that spatial catastrophes from temporary shocks are not a central tendency, favouring locational fundamentals | Davis & Weinstein (2002), [LIT-2205](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2205.md), read from NBER w8517 in [NOTE-1696](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1696.md), not from the AER version of record. The sharp edges: the coefficients are the working paper's (−1.048 for 1947–60; −0.759 and −1.027 with the prewar trend for 1960 and 1965); the instruments assume bombing did not target growth; the outcome is population share only; locational fundamentals are inferred from the reversion, not measured; and reversion within the observed shocks cannot exclude thresholds beyond them. | Active |
| [THEORY-1503](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1503.md) v2 | Davis and Weinstein find, testing unique against multiple equilibria by threshold regression on the Allied bombing of Japanese cities, that city population, the city share of aggregate manufacturing and city-industry output pooled over eight manufacturing industries tend to return after the shock to their prior shares: the Schwarz criterion prefers a single equilibrium for manufacturing and for city-industry output; for population it slightly prefers two equilibria, but that fit, like the best two-equilibrium fit for industries, fails the requirement that larger negative shocks lead to lower equilibria; and pooled city-industry shares were still recovering in 1969, which the authors suggest may be because the hardest-hit places take longer, though without Hiroshima the persistence is indistinguishable from zero | Davis & Weinstein (2004 working paper; J. Limits: the test assumes each city's dynamics depend on its own share alone and that thresholds are common in log units across cities and industries; it imposes full reversion in the threshold runs; it has little power for single industries; and it bears on recovery of established places, not on whether new support can make a place. | Active |
| [THEORY-1508](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1508.md) v2 | Chetty, Hendren and Katz find, in the Moving to Opportunity experiment, that a housing voucher requiring a family in high-poverty public housing to move to a low-poverty tract for its first year raised the adult earnings of children who moved before age 13 by about 31% at ages 24 and over, that the gain fell by about $364 a year for each year of age at the move and was absent or negative for those who moved as teenagers, and that their parents’ earnings were unchanged however long they lived in lower-poverty areas; the authors conclude that the effect runs through the amount of childhood exposure, not through family income or exposure in adulthood | Chetty, Hendren & Katz (2016), [LIT-2193](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2193.md), read from NBER w21156 (revised September 2015) in [NOTE-1695](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1695.md). Held as what the study finds, with its hedges: earnings are observed only to about age 28; age at move was not randomized, so the per-year gradient is not a causal estimate and the disruption cost is not separately identified; older-child estimates are imprecise. The voucher was standing support, held indefinitely while income stayed low; only the first-year low-poverty restriction and counselling were transient, so this is persistence after the end of childhood exposure, not after support was withdrawn. | Active |
| [THEORY-1517](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1517.md) v2 | Knack finds, across 80 aid-receiving countries from 1982 to 1995, that higher mean aid relative to GNP or to government spending goes with smaller gains in the ICRG governance index, controlling for initial governance, income growth and population growth; the effect roughly doubles when aid is instrumented with recipient need and donor interest, holds within sub-Saharan Africa for aid relative to GNP, is several times larger for technical assistance, does not depend on initial governance, and shrinks as aid becomes less predictable | Knack (2000), [LIT-2219](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2219.md), read in [NOTE-1707](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1707.md) in its World Bank working-paper version; the 2001 journal version was not read. | [THEORY-1529](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1529.md) | Human cooperation is readily sustained between individuals, above all in dyads, through precise reciprocity, empathy and a partner who cannot be excluded at no cost, and is fragile between groups: categorization alone yields mistrust and in-group favouritism by bounded reciprocity, observed out-group favouritism hardens it into distrust, and chiefly negative interdependence, real or perceived, turns that into costly competition, aggression and hate, so that the processes that build in-group cooperation can fuel intergroup conflict | The thesis Van Lange and Bergmann (2026), [LIT-2002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2002.md), propose, filed beside the Active report [THEORY-1352](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1352.md) by the twenty-seventh status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md), [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1497](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1497.md) holds that he holds it; whether it is true is this entry's question, under the condition [THEORY-1497](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1497.md) carried, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1550](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1550.md) | An international gift its recipient cannot repay leaves the recipient inferior and the relation resentful, and circular (kula-like) reciprocity that lets the recipient give back is the better design for aid between nations | The thesis Heins, Unrau and Avram (2018), [LIT-2178](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2178.md), carry from Mauss and Dillon, split from [THEORY-1474](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1474.md) when the twenty-eighth status review promoted the report of it ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1474](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1474.md) holds that they hold and report it; whether it is true is this entry's question, under the condition [THEORY-1474](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1474.md) carried, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1569](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1569.md) | Gardiner argues that climate change joins a global commons problem to an intergenerational one that institutions and reciprocity cannot solve, because the generations do not coexist, and that these, with our theories' weakness, leave each generation open to moral corruption that hides its exploitation of its temporal position, even from itself | Gardiner (2006), read in full ([NOTE-1252](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1252.md)). A short programmatic paper: the Pure Intergenerational Problem is drawn from his 2003 paper, which the record does not hold, and seven of the eight corruption strategies are only named. It concerns why policy is hard to make, not what a just policy is, and says nothing about the self. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1574](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1574.md) | Bostrom argues that on aggregative, time-neutral views of value reducing existential risk is a global priority, and that it is undersupplied for lack of motivation as well as understanding, since its benefit is a pan-generational public good whose future beneficiaries cannot pay and moral sentiment is insensitive to scope | Bostrom (2013), read in full from the published version ([NOTE-1321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1321.md)). The longtermist text that says most about motivation. Maxipok holds "whenever we act out of an impersonal concern for humankind as a whole", and Bostrom grants that "Unrestricted altruism is not so common" (p. 19). The risk estimates are subjective, and the motivational diagnosis is theory, not tested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1623](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1623.md) | Ord reports that since The Precipice existential risk from climate change has fallen, risk from nuclear war has risen, and risk from pandemics and from AI has moved in no clear direction, so that none of the book's rounded per-century estimates has moved far | Ord's talk of February 2024, posted July 2024, read in full ([NOTE-1317](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1317.md)) in place of The Precipice. No references and no new numbers: directions of change only, and the overall one in six this century is not restated. Its use is as the author's restatement of the book's headline estimates. | Proposed |
